messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Marisol is a 74-year-old Latina woman who has been married for eleven years to her second husband and works part-time as a pharmacist at a community pharmacy in the city where she has lived for the past two decades. She came to the initial intake appointment alone, dressed carefully, and spoke in measured sentences that occasionally broke apart when she reached certain words — *family*, *home*, *weak* — as though the words themselves had edges she was trying not to touch.

The abuse began approximately three years into her first marriage, decades ago, but the episode that brought her to treatment was more recent: a sustained period of physical violence inflicted by her first husband during a visit he made to her home — uninvited, years after their divorce — when she was in her late sixties. He had come to the door without warning. She remembered the sound of it opening before she had time to reach the lock, and then the particular quality of the silence just before he spoke. What followed lasted less than an hour, but Marisol carries it now as a series of fixed images — her hand against the kitchen counter, the angle of the light through the window, the specific position of her body on the floor — each one preserved with the hard clarity of a photograph. When those images surface, she does not merely recall them. Her body folds into the same posture she held then, shoulders drawn inward, arms crossing her torso, as though the memory arrives not in her mind but in her muscles.

In the weeks after the incident, Marisol found herself listening. She would stand in the hallway of her own home and track every sound — a car door outside, the furnace clicking on, any shift in the air that might mean the front door was moving. She has come to treat the interior of her house as a place that offers no guarantee of safety, and she monitors it accordingly. Her body, she says, never fully releases. There is a baseline tension she has stopped expecting to leave.

Over the following months, a quieter erosion set in. Marisol began declining invitations from her daughter and grandchildren, first occasionally and then almost entirely. When her daughter made a passing comment about the family gathering for the holidays, Marisol felt something close to dread — not grief, but a kind of bracing, as though the mention of family had become inseparable from the circumstances in which family had failed to protect her. She had come to believe that allowing anyone to come close to her emotionally was a form of exposure she could not afford, and so she held her husband at a careful distance, answered his concern with brevity, and told herself this was simply how she was now.

At work, the consequences became harder to conceal. Marisol has been a pharmacist for over forty years, a profession she chose because it required precision, knowledge, and the capacity to be trusted with other people's wellbeing. But she found herself struggling to concentrate during consultations, distracted by the sound of the pharmacy's back door — a heavy door that staff used for deliveries and that opened with a particular force. Each time it slammed, she would stop mid-sentence. Colleagues noticed. She began scheduling herself only for shifts when that door was unlikely to be used, and she stopped taking the longer patient consultations she had once handled with ease. She was certain, in a way she could not argue herself out of, that she was no longer the pharmacist she had been — that whatever had defined her professionally had been taken from her, or had revealed itself to have been fragile all along.

What finally brought Marisol to seek help was not a single event but a slow accumulation of loss: the faith she had once placed in people, in the order of things, in the idea that a life built carefully would hold. When she remembers what happened, the emotion that rises most forcefully is not anger but shame — a deep, private conviction that she should have prevented it, that her inability to do so confirmed something she fears has always been true about her. What she most hopes for, she said quietly at the end of the intake session, is to feel capable again. What she most fears is that she will not.
